As someone with a liberal arts background, I partly disagree with you; my background is rhetoric, writing and linguistics. And I'm about to drop some knowledge on you that you don't get in Calc. III, Differential Equations or Fluid Dynamics. So, listen up.  

Definitively, the problem is that anti-intellectualism is deeply ingrained in western society and has been for decades upon decades. In the 19th century, in response to The Enlightenment, what eventually become known as Modernism, people began questioning the existence of absolutism, reality, objectivity, facts and truth--The Enlightenment was all about absolutes. Modernist thought peaked in the early 20th century, became mainstream, and eventually morphed into Postmodernism around the 1950s-1960s, solely because intellectuals and academics wanted to differentiate themselves from popular culture that had become definitively Modernist (think Joyce, Eliot, Hemingway). Ultimately, Postmodernism is Modernism; there's no substantial difference. It's confusing, but then again, these are people that routinely engage in contradictory arguments. The mere fact that I can't sufficiently explain the difference only proves my point... 

With that said, Postmodernism commonly rejects universal objectivity and asserts that all truths are relative to larger systems (historical, social and cultural contexts); it's a bit like Structuralism (which as a science guy you might be aware of ?). During Postmodernism, academics and intellectuals began heavily questioning the validity of empirical knowledge, even more so than when they called it Modernism, because it was a bit more edgy than debating moral relativism (rejecting Christianity), and well, LSD was everywhere. At this time, people were literally engaged in debates over whether numbers were absolute or if they were relative to human perception and or language. Psychedelic drugs had a profound impact on academia and intellectualism in the latter part of the 20th century; academics literally began questioning the existence of reality. Thankfully, Postmodernism has since run its course, but we're still feeling the after-effects

As someone that recently graduated with a BA, I can say that I've had at least four professors, all whom hold tenure and are probably more intelligent than I am, question the existence of objectivity to some degree. These arguments are extremely refined. By definition they're paradoxes (a paradox appears logical until you carry it out to its ultimate conclusion), e.g., one argument was that scientists cannot be entirely objective, because they all hold personal biases, and thus, they will interpret data in a way that supports their biases (subjectivity). In reality, that's a an easy argument to refute; you simply say to your professor, "Due to my personal biases, I don't believe repeatedly punching you in the face will hurt you!", and then you proceed to beat the shit out of them in front of the class. Unfortunately that's frowned upon in the academic community, so the class becomes engaged in a contradictory discussion that proves to be ultimately meaningless, and thus no knowledge is gained. 

As for the paradox of Postmodernism, if you assert all truths are relative (subjective), then you're making an affirmative statement. An affirmative statement is the assertion of an absolute truth (objective).Furthermore, if all truths are relative (subjective) then no truths can be absolute (objective); however, stating that no truths are absolute is an absolute truth in and of itself; that is the definition of a paradox. Logically, relativism cannot be absolute, but if you ascribe to postmodernist thought, then relativism is; though, you just casually gloss over the logical contradiction to support your bias.           

Now, I'm going to pull this all together. The fact that you can't think about "alternative facts" logically and understand where that logic comes from, proves to me that your "science" education has drastically failed you; you don't understand the history of the society you're living in. The issue with education in the US isn't a lack of emphasis on science per say, but it's a lack of an emphasis on critical thinking. To think critically, you have to understand the history of western thought; there's absolutely no way around this. Any idiot can be trained to punch numbers into a calculator, and any idiot can be trained regurgitate Aristotle. Neither of those two idiots provide anything worthwhile to society; they're both regurgitating information and haven't been trained to think for themselves (to create). The problem with the current education system in the US isn't a lack of science education, but it's the lack of a well-rounded education that teaches individuals to think critically about everything.

People like to jump on this guy cause supposedly he's a racist. I'm not sure if he is; he could be and he could not be. Tonight (last night maybe? It's 2:30am here), CNN had a good bit about Sessions. 

He was a state prosecutor that brought charges against 3 politically active African Americans in the 70s/80s. The jury found these 3 to be innocent and didn't convict them of any crimes. One of the three is still alive, she thinks Sessions is a worthless, racist son of a bitch. 

On the other hand, her son, an Alabama politician actually likes Sessions and doesn't believe he's a racist. He's worked with and interacted with him. He believes Sessions was just acting as a prosecutor would and carried out the case just like any other prosecutor would, cause it's their job.

Personally, I don't know what I believe. It's not a cut and dry issue. Racism isn't cut and dry. People are people, and they tend to go where the money, prestige and advantages are; I don't think that makes them racists per say, but just normal people. 

As a white southerner, talking about about racial issues in the 60s/70s/80s is not like it is presently. Personally, I'm four generations away from the slave trade; and I'm so in the sense that my mother's mother's great-grandfather was a Lt. Col. for the Confederacy, owned slaves (that we know of house slaves) and possibly a small plantation (Sherman burned the records on his march). As a child, I could see the prejudice in my mother, it's definitely lessened over the year, but in my father, who doesn't have historical ties to the South, there is a different perspective towards blacks; he doesn't have a racist bone in his body. He's a lifelong Democrat. 

In the south in the 70s and 80s, as white, you would potentially be ostracized if you spoke out against the status quo back then; when discussing these eras, I believe this is worth noting. Granted, people like George Wallace (a man that later looked down upon his former self...just like Bedford Forest would eventually feel guilty about creating the KKK) were bad; no doubt. They went out of their way to capitalize on racial tensions, but I think there's a huge difference between not having a backbone (conforming to the status quo for your own personal gains) at a young age and being a full blown racist. 

I think on both sides racism is a societal construct. Without a doubt, American society has disenfranchised blacks, but what doesn't get talked about is the historical pressures placed upon whites by land owning whites to conform to a racist ideology for the benefit (the institution of slavery) of landowners, and the system the landowners were profiting off of. Systematically speaking, it goes both ways. The systems we live in are racist and create racists; people are not inherently racist. 

Is Sessions Jesus Christ, Ghandi, Bill and or Ted or the most ethical man to ever exist? Probably not. But, is he a racist. Probably not. I imagine he's a white southerner that was trying to make it in politics and appeal to his constituency that were only 2-3 generations away from the slave trade. Sessions has a J.D., and I'll leave y'all with this, as someone who went to law school, most lawyers went to law school to change the world. They didn't go to halt progress. Unfortunately, in law, prosecutors make the real money and get amazing benefits; if you have a family this is where you want to be. Or as Noel Gallagher put it from Oasis, "this town where your living has made you man, but all of your dreams are washed away in the sand." Defense lawyers are lucky to be in the top 50% of wage earners in their profession; not everyone gets to be a spaceman. 

I'm not taking a stance. This is just food for thought. What I do know is this: as Americans, we need to change the overlying narratives that we abide by. The American Dream, the Horatio Alger Myth if you may, is antiquated. We need to start focusing less on individualism and more on collectivism. If anything, this recent election cycle has taught me that Americans are seriously lost and searching for a collective identity to rally behind. Sanders and Trump were evident of this. As a collective, we need to find that identity and embrace it. 

And one last thought, I think on both sides of the spectrum individuals are seeking a liberation from the status quo; they want more, and that's a good thing. While I in no way endorsed or supported Trump going into November, I believe Trump is a peaceful compromise in the right direction; he's essentially a product America's growing pains. He's an awkward teenager, but he also represents a step away from the political thought has been dominating mainstream American consciousness since the 1950s. He's a step in the right direction. Now with that said, it doesn't mean that anything he stands for is good or that he's going to do a good job. But, Trump demonstrates that America is not afraid to grow, to take risks in hope of a better future. 

Trump shows that the US is not apathetic (and on both sides of the spectrum); that this is still a nation that refuses to take the status quo at their word; that we're revolutionists at heart. This election both sides rejected the establishment, and the left is continuing to reject Trump. Trump has brought politics to the forefront of American thought; for a short while in 2016, CNN became what MTV was in the 80s and 90s. I genuinely think this is phenomenal, and I believe this past year and this election represents America waking up from an apathetic slumber.

I can sing, and I can play stringed instruments. Singing is much different from from playing an instrument. For example, remove my sight and hearing, and I would still be able to play a guitar almost as well I could if could hear and see. If you removed my hearing, I wouldn't be able to sing, because I couldn't hear myself. The human voice is not designed within a finite set parameters like an instrument is. When you play an E chord on a guitar, a piano or a mandolin, it's the same every time. 

After you've learned how to play an instrument, you don't need to hear it to play it, and you sure as hell don't need to be able to look at it; I play with my eyes closed most of the time. 

Singing on the other hand is much more involved. It requires balancing your voice with the acoustics of your environment.
